speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Arts education, as we know, takes place both in schools, as well as in the public domain and I will be covering both in my speech today.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us may not be very inclined to see a career in the arts as something that is lucrative, or the doing of "creative things" as "useful" or "prestigious".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are other "more pressing" national priorities, more "bread-and-butter" issues, which deserve our attention.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Certainly, whenever I speak in this House about the arts, the online commentators seem to agree and I often get comments to say: "Why does this Member always want to speak about the arts?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Can she not talk about more bread-and-butter issues?" Mr Speaker, I would go so far as to say that developing a creative citizenry is a bread-and-butter issue.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Outdated societal views that the arts and creativity are "less important" are changing.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent press release, the Ministry of Education (MOE) has noted that our students believed that it was possible to be creative in different disciplines.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are also potentially positive effects on Singapore's economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is one of the top five critical core skills that has been identified as "essential for the Singapore workforce to be competitive globally." Countries all over the world are also struggling to deal with developments in artificial intelligence and with societal polarisation across racial, religious and socio-economic fault lines.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Solutions to these problems as well, will have to be devised not just book-smarts, but with creativity and empathy too.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, how do we go about "developing" this creativity?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: That is where a robust arts education comes into play.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The United Nations Education, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Framework for Culture and Arts Education recognises that culture and arts play a vital role in the flourishing of human imagination, creativity and self-expression.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A large component of arts education is, of course, the education that we receive through our schools.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My first suggestion for MOE is to add more exposure to theatre and drama education, in our present primary school curriculum.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In many developed countries, drama is an integral part of the national school curriculum.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In engaging with drama educators and the Singapore Drama Educators Association, I have learnt that there are many positive social effects that come out of using drama as a medium of education.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Role-play and other process-driven drama techniques can help pupils to identify with and explore characters and issues.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They help students to become more confident with language and communication.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They also provide opportunities for students to develop and order their ideas, through acting and improvisation of scenes in various settings.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are certainly all skills which are worth developing.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In learning how to articulate their own emotions, students become better communicators and more confident with their use of language to develop and organise their ideas and thoughts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Self-direction, confidence and communication are, of course, all part of the 21st century core competencies which have been identified by MOE itself.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened, however, that MOE has acknowledged that drama is an important pedagogical tool that can be adopted to enhance learning.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A solid drama education may therefore help build on their intrinsic creative abilities, giving them the medium to express themselves well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, someday soon, a similar survey will show that our students have faith in their abilities as storytellers and would-be entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The second suggestion I would like to surface came out of a conversation that I had with Mr Ang Song Ming.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Song Ming was the Singapore's representative at the 58th Venice Biennale and he now lives in Berlin in Germany.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Song Ming asked why can we not think more of arts education as something to be integrated with the core education syllabus, instead of being thought of primarily as a standalone subject.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We can see this "interdisciplinary" nature of the arts in the works of artists like Robert Zhao.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Robert is coincidentally Singapore's Venice Biennale representative for this year.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In his Venice Biennale work, titled "Seeing Forest", Robert looks at "secondary forests" in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, if you did not know, these are forests which have regrown from land that had previously been cleared due to human intervention.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Robert then examines the new ecosystems that have developed within these forests.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Important lessons can be learned from his work on how the island of Singapore has evolved and the ways in which human urban design can shape the natural world.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They have roots in science, geography and environmental issues and when conveyed in the context of artworks, allow students to imagine and dream of possibilities beyond the confines of academic book-learning.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, one day we could see Robert's work and research being taught alongside the academic content of a Science or Geography lesson?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To be fair, arts educators tell me this kind of interdisciplinary learning already happens in schools.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But I understand that this is largely on an ad hoc basis, for example, when teachers of other academic subjects proactively decide to engage in "cross-over" projects with their art-trained colleagues.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But more fundamentally – and this brings me to my next point – arts education in schools cannot thrive, if arts educators themselves are feeling unsupported or disillusioned.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In the course of speaking to arts educators, members of my research team and I encountered some troubling sentiments.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the teachers we spoke to seemed to sense that they were viewed as "less important", or somehow lower in the "pecking order" of teachers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Arts teachers have also told us things like how they are sometimes expected, as a matter of course and with very little respect, to execute anything and everything that is "aesthetic" in schools.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This can range from stage and plant pot arrangements in prize-giving ceremonies, to general embellishments and decorations around the campus.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As one teacher told me rather sadly, "We do not go to art school   to get a degree in how to make decorations." All of this put together can result in low morale on the part of arts teachers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If schools and other subject teachers perpetuate the notion that arts subjects are not as important as other subjects, students and parents will get the same impression.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Students therefore become less focused and less interested during their classes and this creates a self-fulfilling and damaging cycle where arts lessons are de-prioritised.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One fallacy that arts teachers face is the thinking that because their work somehow involves less marking in the traditional sense, it therefore requires much less effort to convey.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: What people may not realise is that arts subjects, just like all subjects, involve a large body of technical skills and subject matter expertise.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On a day-to-day basis, arts teachers are also often responsible for studio space and equipment.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Significant amounts of time may need to be spent accounting for, maintaining and enhancing those spaces.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, this is not a competition as to what kind of teacher has a more difficult time.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: All teachers, whether arts teachers or non-arts teachers, face heavy teaching responsibilities from grading, lesson planning and pastoral care duties.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am an educator myself and I understand full well the difficulties that all teachers face today.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I simply want to point out today that arts teachers face their own unique set of challenges that are sometimes overlooked.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have also heard feedback that there can be inconsistency in whether arts teachers are allowed by schools to continue on with their own public-facing arts practices.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It can be demoralising for teachers to be told that they cannot continue with developing their own practices, especially if they view their own arts practices as important for their roles as educators.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It would be good if consistent, clear and transparent policies are rolled out across the board.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It should be clear as to whether, when and to what extent teachers in primary schools, secondary schools and junior colleges can continue to maintain their own creative practices.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, actual working artists come into schools, to help with teaching and curriculum planning.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This not only eases some of the burdens on art teachers but also gives students important practical insights into what the interesting and varied life of a working artist can look like.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many arts educators who have left full-time teaching to pursue other ambitions and dreams continue to have an interest in education.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is both inspirational value in this for students, as well as potential respite for the overworked and full-time educators in the field.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Just over the past weekend, I attended a performance by the Asian Cultural Symphony Orchestra which performed original classical pieces composed in response to different neighbourhoods in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It was a lovely performance in the lead-up to National Day.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There was a piece composed for Geylang Serai, one for Toa Payoh, one for Tiong Bahru and so on.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This was accompanied with images of the neighbourhood as the musicians performed.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It was a great example of how classical music can be contextualised and made relevant to the public at large, without being over-simplified.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the PABL will continue and eventually be expanded to include more of such diverse local groups.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Presently, I understand the scheme includes a curated list of arts groups but I hope that eventually, it will be opened to more applicants who wish to join the scheme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Outside of the academic school syllabus, our museums, private institutions and arts groups also do important work in arts education in the public domain.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, our public artworks are often the first significant points of contact that members of the public have with art.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In this area, there are some low-hanging fruit in terms of additional steps that we can take in improving the educational value of our public art.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The primary one I want to focus on is this: better policies on the labelling of our public artworks.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, this should be enforced whenever art is displayed publicly.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans have also recently spoken up on this point.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Art historian and academic, Jeffrey Say, for example, has opined in a letter to The Straits Times on 15 July that: "Proper attribution shows we value the work of the artist and the role of the artwork in the community and in placemaking." Government institutions are places visited by legislators, civil servants and members of the public.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If the art and historical objects displayed there are explained to these visitors, these buildings then turn into mini-museums.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This has the potential to educate people as they go about their everyday business.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Parliament House itself is an illustrative case in point.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: How many of us in this Chamber know that the large painting by the late Dr Lai Kui Fang outside the Parliament library, depicts the swearing-in of Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his first cabinet in 1959?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If we squint very hard, we may see the name of the artist on the bottom of the frame.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But do we know that the work was painted entirely based on oral and archival history, because there were no photographic records of the event?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The attention to detail in the painting is exquisite.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The lines are finely-rendered and the interplay of shadows makes the work look alive.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The painting is infused with the sense of energy that one can only imagine would have been in the air, in the founding years of our nation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: How many of us know that some of the busts that line the corridor outside this very Chamber were made by sculptor Dora Gordine, a female artist who has also sculpted local war heroine Elizabeth Choy?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Gordine was herself lauded as a "genius" in a Straits Times article of 5 August 1932, when her works were acquired for the Singapore Municipal Building.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This article, back in 1932, mind you, observed that the acquisition made Singapore an "art centre of Asia".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, we might ask, why is information like this even important?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Well, it offers us another unique and imaginative lens through which we can view our shared history.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It helps us to build connections with one another.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Visual and emotional stimulation such as this, allows us to develop a shared affective bond about our country.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that is not quantifiable in dollars and cents, but it is also something which is absolutely priceless.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to pause to convey my particular thanks to Mr Speaker who, when I raised some of these issues with him, has been very open to receiving feedback about better labelling of the art in this House.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: When contextualised, the Samsui Woman mural struck a chord with Singaporeans, who felt that the work honestly depicted these women at rest.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Singer Inch Chua, herself a descendant of a Samsui woman, commented in a Straits Times article by journalist Shawn Hoo on 20 July, that she loved the mural of the young lady, observing that it was like, seeing her great-grandmother's rebellious teenage photos.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To her, this was something that was both eye-opening and delightful.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With the Raffles and Wallich colonial statues at Fort Canning, while I am quite aware that decolonisation as a political movement took place many decades ago, the term "decolonisation" is also used today to describe a push to re-examining colonial legacies, particularly, where these colonial legacies tend to gloss over the stories of the indigenous people of those places.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many museums and institutions all over the world, including the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Britain itself, are re-examining their colonial legacies.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As Straits Times Correspondent Clement Yong observed in his article of 3 July 2024, the legacy of Stamford Raffles is complicated.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It includes, amongst others, Raffles' ostensible involvement in the Massacre Of Palembang in 1811.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The point of "decolonisation", used in this modern sense, is not to gloss over these complications.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But to acknowledge them, observe them objectively and critically, and learn from them.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, to me, the statues in Fort Canning are not necessarily blindly laudatory of colonial legacies.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If Members look at the statues and I encourage everyone to do so if Members have not done so, Members will see that the colonial figures here, are blending into and almost dissolving into the foliage around them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MOE is committed to developing students holistically, in the moral, intellectual, social, physical and aesthetic dimensions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Arts education is an integral part of holistic education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Through arts education, we aim to nurture learners who appreciate the arts, express themselves creatively, think critically, embrace ambiguity and welcome diverse perspectives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Over the years, we have strengthened arts education in our schools and higher education institutions, establishing a suite of provisions to cater to students with varying levels of interest and ability.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Besides Art and Music lessons, lower primary students have additional exposure to the arts through the Programme for Active Learning (PAL).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Those with greater interest in the arts may join arts Co-Curricular Activities (CCAs) in their schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: At upper secondary and pre-university, students who are passionate about the arts can pursue them as an elective subject.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Some schools offer specialised arts programmes, such as the Art or Music Elective Programme, or the more recently introduced Enhanced Art or Music Programme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In fact, schools also engage professional performing arts groups and artists to provide exposure to various art forms and cultivate appreciation at the cohort, course and CCA levels.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The School of the Arts, established in 2008, provides an alternative pathway for students demonstrating talent and interest in the arts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Beyond the school system, students can choose over 80 publicly funded arts and design related courses across various Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In our international scans, we find that our arts curriculum standards and teaching methods are on par with those of other developed nations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our arts syllabuses are updated regularly to feature contemporary works, as well as pieces from diverse cultures, including works by local artists and musicians.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The wide repertoire serves as a rich tapestry of inspiration for our students and demonstrates to our students that they, too, can be creators in the arts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our revised arts curriculum empowers students to go beyond appreciating the works of artists and musicians, to creating and communicating their own ideas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This allows them to be immersed in a diverse range of creative experiences, from activities that foster critical thinking in PAL drama lessons to innovative art and music projects at the primary and lower secondary levels.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For instance, in a primary school art lesson, students are challenged to consider how narratives presented in artworks can be enhanced by accompanying soundscapes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Lower secondary music lessons introduce students to digital tools for recording and performing their compositions, showcasing their artistic voice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The arts CCAs provide platforms for students to present their creative works through exhibitions, concerts, dance performances and theatrical productions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Ms Chandradas mentioned overcoming siloed approaches in implementation, by encouraging cooperation across institutions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We have, in recent years, forged more partnerships with Government agencies and the arts industry to provide our students with exposure to real-world artistic experiences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In partnership with the National Arts Council (NAC), our Museum-Based Learning and Performing Arts-Based Learning help to bridge classroom learning and real-world artistic practice for our Primary 4 and lower secondary students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Schools are also deepening their partnerships with Singapore arts professionals to co-design and deliver bespoke arts learning experiences for their students, with the support of NAC's AISS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In 2024, schools are rolling out over 100 AISS projects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In addition, students in our Enhanced Art Programme schools are mentored by our local artists in collaboration with Nanyang Polytechnic, while budding songwriters from our schools are mentored by local songwriters in the Singapore Youth Festival.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We have made good progress in developing students' creativity, not just through arts education but through total curriculum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our students, regardless of social-economic status, demonstrated the ability to generate original and diverse ideas for a wide range of problem-solving tasks and contexts, which required expression and imagination.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: They also reported favourable perceptions of their teachers' pedagogies, which helped in nurturing their creativity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our students' performance in the study is testament to the impact of our curriculum design and teaching approaches in fostering creativity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will continue to review our curriculum regularly to ensure its relevance in preparing our students for the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We agree that including drama in our primary school curriculum can build students' confidence, communication skills and other important competencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Drama strategies are used in different subjects to make learning more enriching.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For example, in primary English Language class, students may take part in the "hot seat" activity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: They step into the shoes of different characters from a story and answer questions of the characters' actions and decisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This helps them understand the story better by seeing things from the characters' perspectives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The ability to engage in meaningful discussions about artworks is a fundamental aspect of our art syllabuses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We regularly feature contemporary artworks that generate discussions that go beyond the arts to other disciplines and global issues.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will continue to explore how more we can enhance connections across disciplines meaningfully while ensuring that knowledge and skills within each discipline are not diluted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: At the heart of quality arts education, are our arts teachers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MOE values our arts teachers, whose passion and hard work play a crucial role in holistic education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MOE is committed to supporting them as well as former teachers who wish to return, whether full-time, part-time or adjunct terms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We appreciate our arts teachers' unwavering commitment to go above and beyond to develop our students; foster creativity; and multi-disciplinary learning, to enable our students to flourish.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We applaud their tireless efforts in nurturing the artistic growth of our students and enriching their educational journey.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In our commitment to supporting arts teachers, it is important we understand how they are evaluated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Over the years, we have enhanced the support provided to arts teachers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This includes, centrally developing teaching resources, offering more professional development opportunities, fostering learning communities among arts teachers across schools and facilitating collaborations with arts professionals to enhance teaching.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Schools can also engage vendors to conduct workshops and excursions, in different art forms, for their students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will continue to explore other ways to support our arts teachers, including their workload.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Ms Chandradas asked about arts teachers continuing their own practice outside of schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MOE encourages our arts teachers to continue being practitioners, as it helps them teach better.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: To celebrate the identity of Art and Music teachers as artists and musicians, MOE provides annual national platforms for our Art and Music teachers to showcase their creative explorations and expressions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Some Art and Music teachers also engage in external performances, gigs, exhibitions as a way to keep in touch with their practice.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We also must enable arts students to connect with one another, with others in the community as well as society.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: And finally, we want our Arts students to be able to contribute to the lives of others by using their creativity to communicate their ideas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: And with that, we will nurture a generation of creative thinkers, connectors and contributors who will help shape our Singapore society and bring our nation forward.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are two days away from our National Day, so let me take this opportunity to wish everyone a Happy National Day in advance.
